finalText:
All 4 tests pass. Here's what happened.

## Root cause

`src/jobs/processOrder.js` acquired a connection and released it on the *success path only*:

```js
const conn = pool.acquire();
const result = await run(conn, order);  // rejects for a bad order
pool.release(conn);                     // never reached on rejection
```

When `run` rejected, the `await` threw and the `pool.release(conn)` line was skipped. `Pool` has no finalizer or timeout reclaim (noted right in `src/db/pool.js:3-5`), so each failed order permanently burned one of the 5 connections.

## The logs confirm it exactly

`worker.log` shows **125 jobs started, 120 released** — 5 missing, precisely the pool size. Every leak steps the gauge up 5ms after an `invalid order payload` failure, and it never steps back down:

| Failure | Gauge |
|---|---|
| `02:06:15.640 order-4122 failed: invalid order payload` | `02:06:15.645 pool in-use: 3/5` |
| `02:06:20.440 order-4123 failed: invalid order payload` | `02:06:20.445 pool in-use: 4/5` |
| `02:06:30.040 order-4125 failed: invalid order payload` | `02:06:30.045 pool in-use: 5/5` |

The tell is that it's a **monotonic ratchet, not saturation** — the one dip-free reading at `02:06:25.245` (4/5, no preceding failure) was a healthy in-flight job that *did* return its connection. Only failures leaked. Two earlier failures at `01:56:11` and `01:58:47` account for the pool already sitting at 2/5 when the burst began.

Once the 5th leaked at `02:06:30`, the next jobs died instantly with `pool exhausted`, and `worker-1` gave up at `02:06:35`. The API's own cascade (`acquire timeout` from `02:11:16`, supervisor restarts at `02:13:36`) is downstream of the same drained pool.

## The fix

`src/handlers/api.js` was already correct — it routes through `withConnection`, whose `finally` always releases. That's why the API-path test passed while the worker tests failed. `processOrder` now uses the same helper:

```js
async function processOrder(pool, order, run) {
  return withConnection(pool, (conn) => run(conn, order));
}
```

The stale comment claimed the direct `acquire` was needed to hold a connection across a retry loop — that loop was already removed, so the exemption had outlived its reason. Left a note to that effect so it doesn't get reintroduced.

## Worth flagging

The fix stops the bleeding, but two things made a single missing `release` escalate into a page, and both are still open:

- **`Pool` has no safety net.** Any future direct `acquire()` leaks permanently. A timeout-based reclaim, or making `withConnection` the only exported way to get a connection, would turn this class of bug from an outage into a logged warning.
- **The gauge was alarming from `02:06:10`, six minutes before the API started failing and seven before the restarts.** A monotonic-rise alert on `pool in-use` (as opposed to a threshold on 5/5) would have caught this while there was still headroom.

Happy to take on either if you want.
